content: Darunavir, when co-administered with ritonavir and other antiretroviral agents, is used for the treatment of HIV infection. For treatment-naïve or treatment-experienced patients without darunavir resistance-associated substitutions, the recommended dose is 800 mg of darunavir with 100 mg of ritonavir taken orally once daily with food. For treatment-experienced patients with at least one darunavir-associated mutation or when genotyping is not available, the dose is 600 mg of darunavir with 100 mg of ritonavir taken orally every 12 hours with food. In treatment-experienced patients, it is recommended to assess the drug susceptibility of the HIV-1 virus through treatment history, genotypic, and/or phenotypic testing. Before initiating darunavir, appropriate laboratory testing, such as serum liver biochemistries, should be obtained. Patients with underlying chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or elevated pretreatment liver enzymes should be monitored for elevated transaminases, particularly during the first several months of treatment. The safety and efficacy of darunavir in children under 3 years of age or weighing ≤10 kg have not been established. Darunavir must always be taken with food. Darunavir interacts with numerous medications due to its effect on hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. These interactions can lead to increased or decreased drug levels, potentially causing serious or life-threatening reactions. Below are specific interactions and recommendations: 1. Contraindicated Medications: Alfuzosin: Increased levels may cause serious reactions. Aprepitant: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Carbamazepine: Decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance. Cobimetinib: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Conivaptan: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Dihydroergotamine (intranasal): Increased levels may cause ergot toxicity. Dronedarone: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Elbasvir/Grazoprevir: Increased levels may cause ALT elevations. Eliglustat: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Flibanserin: Increased levels may cause severe hypotension or syncope. Fosaprepitant: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Irinotecan (and liposomal): Increased levels may cause toxicity. Isavuconazonium sulfate: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Ivabradine: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Lomitapide: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Lovastatin: Increased levels may cause rhabdomyolysis. Lurasidone: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Mavacamten: Increased levels may cause heart failure due to systolic dysfunction. Methylergonovine: Increased levels may cause ergot toxicity. Naloxegol: Increased levels may precipitate opioid withdrawal symptoms. Pacritinib: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Phenobarbital: Decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance. Phenytoin: Decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance. Pimozide: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Ranolazine: Increased levels may cause serious reactions. Regorafenib: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Rifampin: Decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance. Salmeterol: Increased levels may cause toxicity. Simvastatin: Increased levels may cause rhabdomyolysis. St. John’s Wort: Decreases darunavir levels, risking therapeutic failure and resistance. Triazolam: Increased levels may cause prolonged sedation or respiratory depression. Venetoclax: Contraindicated during the initial ramp-up phase due to increased toxicity risk. Voclosporin: Increased levels may cause toxicity. 2. Medications Requiring Dose Adjustments or Monitoring: Acalabrutinib: Avoid or interrupt treatment if co-administration is necessary. Adagrasib: Avoid until steady-state concentrations are reached. Afatinib: Reduce the dose by 10 mg if not tolerated. Apixaban: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors. Avanafil: Avapritinib: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Axitinib: Reduce the dose by 50% if co-administration is unavoidable. Bedaquiline: Avoid co-administration for more than 14 consecutive days unless benefits outweigh risks. Bosutinib: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Brigatinib: Reduce the dose by 50% if co-administration is unavoidable. Cabozantinib: Decrease the dose by 40 mg/day (Cometriq) or 20 mg/day (Cabometyx). Capivasertib: Reduce the dose and monitor for adverse effects. Ceritinib: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Copanlisib: Reduce the dose to 45 mg if co-administration is unavoidable. Dabrafenib: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Daridorexant: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Edoxaban: Adjust dose for DVT/PE treatment to 30 mg once daily. Elacestrant: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Encorafenib: Reduce the dose to one-third if co-administration is unavoidable. Entrectinib: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Erdafitinib: Monitor closely for adverse reactions and adjust dose accordingly. Everolimus: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Fedratinib: Reduce the dose to 200 mg/day if co-administration is unavoidable. Felbamate: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Flutamide: Avoid or monitor closely for adverse effects. Fluticasone (intranasal): Monitor for signs of high corticosteroid concentrations. Gilteritinib: Monitor closely for adverse effects and adjust dosage as needed. Glasdegib: Monitor for QTc prolongation and other adverse effects. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir: Avoid co-administration due to increased toxicity risk. Ibrutinib: Avoid co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 3. Special Considerations: Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) and Stem Cell Mobilization: ART medications should not be taken for at least one month before cell mobilization or until all cycles of apheresis are completed, as they may interfere with cell manufacturing. CYP3A4 Substrates: Darunavir significantly affects the metabolism of drugs that are substrates of CYP3A4, necessitating careful monitoring, dose adjustments, or avoidance of co-administration. In summary, darunavir has extensive drug interactions primarily mediated through CYP3A4 metabolism. These interactions necessitate careful consideration of co-administered medications to avoid toxicity, therapeutic failure, or resistance development.
